content: 1. Any modifications to the patient monitoring system must be carefully implemented to ensure that the health center complies with national standards. 2. For HIV patient monitoring, specific roles and responsibilities are assigned to various staff members: Triage workers, receptionists, or data clerks are responsible for maintaining an appointment book, identifying missed appointments, initiating or retrieving patient records, and recording patient data in the appropriate patient record or register, depending on the HIV service provided. ART aides, lay counselors, or professional counselors are tasked with recording patient data in the patient record or register, as applicable to the HIV service provided. Nurses, clinical officers, or other clinicians are required to document patient data in the patient record or register, record information on patient-held cards, books, or passports (if used), tally data, complete routine reports, conduct patient reviews with the clinical team using longitudinal records, discuss patient outcomes, review routine HIV program reports to track progress, assess the quality of HIV services by reviewing registers, and evaluate the quality of HIV patient records and registers in collaboration with the clinical or district supportive supervision team. If a data clerk, secretary, or other staff member is unavailable, clinicians may need to transcribe data from patient records to registers, tally data, and complete routine reports. Data clerks, secretaries, or other staff members are responsible for organizing and managing patient records and registers, transcribing data from patient records to registers, entering patient data into a database (if used), tallying data, completing routine reports, reviewing registers to assess the quality of HIV services and data, and evaluating the quality of HIV patient records and registers with the clinical or district supportive supervision team. Community health workers initiate HIV testing and counseling in the community, monitor adherence and drug pick-up, and follow up with and trace patients lost to care. Pharmacists and pharmacy technicians/assistants dispense medications, manage drug-related toxicities, and provide adherence counseling and monitoring. Facility-based lay providers enroll patients, complete demographic information on cards, transfer information to registers, provide adherence counseling, treatment literacy, and education, assess adherence through methods such as pill counts, and track patients lost to follow-up. 3. Recommendations for strengthening human resource development include integrating training into pre-service education, providing in-service and ongoing training, supporting trainees, and ensuring that staff trained during medical, nursing, pharmacy, or other degree programs focus on refresher courses or continuing education. Opportunities outside formal training, such as case reviews, experience sharing, clinical mentoring, educational presentations, conferences, and cross-site visits, should also be utilized. 4. Clinical mentoring and supportive supervision involve assigning experienced clinicians to provide ongoing training and advice to less experienced providers. This helps build their skills, confidence, and capacity to deliver high-quality care. Mentors meet regularly with providers to review clinical cases, answer questions, solve problems, provide feedback, and assist with case management. These visits may include observing case management, reviewing HIV patient cards and ART registers, conducting clinical case reviews, holding clinical team meetings, and documenting each visit with recommendations. 5. Transitioning from paper to electronic patient monitoring systems is driven by the increasing difficulty of accurately retrieving data from paper-based systems and the time and effort required to maintain them as data volume grows. This transition may involve various levels of electronic data entry, such as electronic medical records (EMRs), electronic registers, or electronic reports generated from paper records. Reliable power, telecommunications, trained staff, and IT technical support are essential for successful implementation. 6. A tiered approach to electronic patient records allows health ministries to strategically implement one of three tiers in facilities offering ART services. This approach ensures harmonized monitoring of routine HIV services and facilitates movement between tiers as resources and infrastructure improve. 7. Improving national and global reporting requires establishing good-quality primary data, minimizing and harmonizing the number of reportable indicators, and ensuring accountability at each administrative level. Reporting frequency should be tailored to the specific indicators being monitored. 8. Country examples demonstrate how patient monitoring tools can be adapted to different settings. For instance, South Africa has implemented a standardized approach to data collection and reporting, with clear timelines and processes for data transmission to higher administrative levels. Responsibilities and accountabilities of different actors are clearly defined. 9. WHO provides guidance on clinical mentoring, patient monitoring systems, and best practices for scaling up HIV care and ART in resource-constrained settings. This includes recommendations for standardizing sentinel events and indicators, de-duplicating records to improve data quality, conducting country situation analyses, and building on patient monitoring systems to enhance HIV case surveillance.
